newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin raps Western media over Yeltsin health.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin raps Western media over Yeltsin health.

text.p: The Kremlin accused Western media on Friday of double standards in their coverage of President Boris Yeltsin's health problems and urged them to abide by a code of dignity and ethics.

"No one tells you -- and certainly no one in the new administration will ever tell you this -- that this (Yeltsin's health) is taboo," Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told a Kremlin briefing.
"This is one of the topics that must be discussed by society and the mass media -- within a certain framework of dignity and ethics."

Yastrzhembsky made clear he believed the media had shown more sympathy towards French president Francois Mitterrand when he was dying of cancer than it had towards Yeltsin, who is preparing in hospital for a heart bypass operation.

"Sometimes I feel like asking you to spare the president, especially the Western media...I believe that -- this is my personal view -- the Western mass media have been using double standards in covering the president's illness," he said.

"If we compare that (media coverage of Mitterrand's illness) with how this (Yeltsin's problem) has been discussed by the Western media, I think there is a considerable difference between the two," he said.

Yastrzhembsky, appointed after Yeltsin's re-election in July, has pledged to pursue a policy of openness on the health of the 65-year-old president, who announced three weeks ago that he planned to have heart surgery.

"I think you should have a minimum of reproaches with regard to the administration's press service over how this topic has been covered. But there are certain limits all the same, from my point of view," he said on Friday.
Western media have been more vigorous in their coverage of Yeltsin's health problems than most of their Russian counterparts and have remained suspicious that the whole truth has not been revealed.

Media in the West made banner headlines out of a suggestion last week by one of the doctors preparing Yeltsin for surgery that the president had a third, unnanounced heart attack just before his re-election.

Kremlin officials said at the time that Yeltsin had a sore throat or a cold and they sought to give the impression throughout the summer that Yeltsin's condition was much less serious than it really was.
Russian media have been somewhat more cautious in their approach and some newspapers have questioned whether the media have gone too far in their coverage.
More than five years after the collapse of communist rule and strict media controls, editors still show extreme care in speculating about the president's health.

The liberal Russian media are particularly wary because Yelsin's health has a huge bearing on the future of Russia's fragile democracy and many journalists fear doing anything which might help the opposition communists return to power.
It was the second time this week that Yastrzhembsky had expressed his reservations about the Western media's coverage.
On Monday he denied allegations published by a British newspaper that Yeltsin had a 50:50 chance of surviving his proposed heart operation and could work only 15 minutes a day.
